<!-- section:why -->

A setting or a compositional rule is useful only when it serves your intention. This lesson helps you explain a choice and inspect its consequence.

<!-- section:understand -->

A shorter exposure time reduces the distance a moving subject travels during exposure, reducing motion blur. It also captures less light under otherwise identical conditions. The desired motion rendering comes first. Test a short and a long exposure, inspect the wheels, then decide whether visible movement helps the story.

<!-- section:see -->

Picture a cyclist crossing the frame. Compare 1/60 second with 1/500 second while holding aperture and scene light constant. The shorter interval records less movement. To maintain the same recorded exposure, another physical exposure input must change; raising ISO instead changes the camera’s signal treatment, not the photons already captured.

<!-- section:deeper -->

A tripod controls camera movement; it cannot freeze a moving cyclist. Panning introduces another creative option and takes practice.

<!-- section:customer -->

Choose a short exposure for a sharp cyclist or a longer exposure for deliberate motion, then check brightness and noise in the result.

<!-- section:try -->

A stationary camera photographs a running dog. You want a sharp face. Choose a shorter or longer time and explain the light tradeoff.

<!-- section:revisit -->

A shorter time is a defensible start for freezing the dog. It admits less light at a fixed aperture; adjust available light or aperture if feasible and inspect the result. The exact time depends on subject speed, distance, and output needs.
